description: We are a motivated team of students interested in space, STEM, and technology.
summary:
We built a physics-based space mission simulator where players design spacecraft and execute orbital maneuvers. “Horizon” is a multiple-user game, with up to 4 users welcomed . Each planet, moon, and star is an original 3D model with physics-accurate calculations. The game's physics - gravity, orbital placement, atmospheric density, and surface radiation - are driven by real NASA data and peer-reviewed scientific models. The game exhibits its own plot that ensures the challenges and creates obstacles throughout the mission; players can choose the level of the given missions and tasks whilst facing the already subtle interferences (limitations in communication, maintenance of the spaceship, and astronomical conditions on individual planets). Alongside that, players learn basic and advanced physics while enjoying the game. Horizon aims to make learning about physics, astronomy, and space exploration more engaging by allowing players to experience these concepts firsthand.
Instead of just reading about scientific principles, players apply them while building spacecraft, managing resources, and solving challenges across different planetary environments.
details:
Entire gameplay and the game's plot are uncovered in Lumini A system: a single-star system, located in the “Upper Arm” of IC486 (SBa-type Galaxy) near a faintly blue region, - region with an amassed number of newborn stars, like Lumini A. Lumini A is the K9V-type star which is 3.67B years. Star has 7 planets (8 if to account Mocha-Mocha's binary twin, - Dott) and 13 unique moons varying from tiny asteroids to spherical major ones to explore.
Players find themselves at the planet Ciosonia as controllers of medium-sized spherical robots called "MechaSphere IR1". In this system, Ciosonian people have decided that losing one of their kind for exploration of outer space is not beneficial. As a result, they have invented spherical robots which include all needed instruments for celestial bodies exploration; however, player will need to upgrade these robots by themselvex to survive in more harsh environments like Methane lakes of Coloss, Dense atmosphere of Hermous Mora, Carbon Dioxide oceans of Tholin, Intense heat on Teanon and tidally locked Quaris or vice versa extremely low temperatures on Mocha-Mocha. Robot upgrades include speed, ability to jump, embedded RCS, better orientation, double protection (From mechanical damage), Radiation/Heat/Acid shields, Hydro-isolation, Improved radio connection, and upgraded visors with Temperature/Night-Vision. In future features, players will be able to customize their MechaSpheres.

3. Environmental Loading: The game loads the body's atmospheric profile and its special calculated conditions. For Titan-analog environments, atmospheric density is modified by high-altitude tholin formation modeled from NASA Cassini space mission findings.

5. Project description: The game proposes four different missions, each one is differentiated by their level of hardness and the plotline. Mission creation was both a creative and research-heavy process, where we had to analyze previous attempts and spatial missions to ensure the accuracy and relevance to real-life events. 

Mission 1 - Colimpri

Story and Background

Сolimpri is one of the moons of the planet, known for its remarkable pink shade and vast “lakes” on the surface. It is the closest celestial body to Ciosonia, and this way it has piqued the interest of scientists.

Сolimpri has next to no atmosphere and extremely low gravity. Because of this, the surface has a varied terrain of cliffs and craters. Different lighting conditions during exploration makes landings extremely difficult.
A number of space probes have made it to orbit, but most of the landers met an unfortunate ending. Difficult terrain and poor visibility caused most of the mishaps.
Even with all of these failures, scientists have pushed for further exploration. The space agency, because of the many money-losing missions, has set a strict budget for СOLIMPRI-21.
With your space exploration skills, the objective is to safely land, explore Сolimpri, and bring back samples to Earth within a strict budget.
Player Objectives
1. Spacecraft Design: Create a spacecraft to transport a science package to Сolimpri and bring a sample back to Earth within the budget. You have to manage the mass, fuel, and size of the science package.
2. Orbital Transfer and Landing: Get to Сolimpri and land in the research zone.
3. Sample Collection: Use the drill and sample container to collect a soil and lake sample.
4. Surface Photography: Use the onboard cameras to take photos of Сolimpri's surface to give scientists their first look at the geology of that moon. Include photos of the surrounding terrain as well.
5. Return to Earth: Secure the samples in a protective container. Once collected, launch the container back to Earth and make sure it lands safely.
Main Gameplay Challenge
Images of Coloss’s outer cloud layers are the only images of the planet available. From these images, scientists cannot conclude much about Coloss’s internal structure, the composition of its atmosphere, or its large-scale features.
The largest interest of scientists is about large, unidentified, atmospheric compounds and giant cloud formations. It’s believed that by understanding these compounds and formations, scientists may be able to learn about how Coloss was formed and evolved. Finding the right balance between cost and performance in spacecraft design.
The player is challenged to work within very tight constraints in designing spacecraft to land and operate on Сolimpri.
Mission 2 – Coloss
Story and Scientific Background


Coloss is an original, scientifically modeled giant planetary body characterized by an exceptionally dense, multilayered atmosphere. Its immense size, powerful atmospheric circulation, and persistent storm systems create significant challenges for planetary observation and exploration.


To investigate this largely unexplored environment, the COLOSS Research Programme was established. Its primary objective is to develop the first comprehensive radar map of Coloss and investigate the structure and chemical composition of its atmosphere.


Participants must design and deploy an orbital research spacecraft capable of maintaining a stable orbit, conducting systematic radar observations, and collecting atmospheric data for scientific analysis.


Player Objectives
Research Spacecraft Design: Construct a spacecraft equipped with a radar system, communication module, and mass spectrometer. Ensure sufficient fuel and operational resources for extended scientific operations.
Orbital Insertion: Deliver the spacecraft to Coloss and establish a stable orbit. Accurate calculations of orbital altitude and velocity are essential to prevent planetary impact or spacecraft loss.
Radar Survey: Conduct systematic radar observations through multiple planned orbital passes to achieve comprehensive planetary coverage.
Planetary Mapping: Process radar data using onboard computers to reveal previously unknown atmospheric structures and geological features represented in the planetary model.
Atmospheric Analysis: Collect and analyse particles from the upper atmospheric layers using a mass spectrometer to investigate their chemical composition.
Scientific Data Return: Transmit the completed radar map and atmospheric measurements to Earth while maintaining sufficient fuel and operational capacity.
Main Gameplay Challenge


Maximize scientific survey coverage while

minimizing fuel consumption.


Participants must optimize orbital trajectories, plan radar scanning sequences, and manage spacecraft resources to achieve the greatest possible scientific return.


Mission 3 – Tholin
Story and Scientific Background


Tholin is an original planetary environment designed around scientific questions in astrobiology and planetary geology. According to its constructed geological scenario, the planet once contained numerous lakes and ponds that may have provided suitable conditions for primitive life billions of years ago.


Although these bodies of water have disappeared, their geological signatures remain preserved in ancient shorelines and surface formations.


Of particular interest is the planet's widespread reddish tholin-rich dust. Its chemical composition and potential toxicity are important factors in assessing environmental hazards for future exploration missions.


An initial research programme deployed multiple robotic rovers to investigate the shorelines of ancient CO₂ lakes. The rovers collected soil, rock, and atmospheric samples, which were sealed in specialized containers and deposited at designated locations for future retrieval.


However, the original sample-return programme became significantly more expensive than anticipated, reaching an estimated cost of 11 billion US dollars, with the projected return date postponed to 2040. Consequently, the programme lost its funding.


Despite its cancellation, the scientific value of the collected samples remained substantial.


A new initiative, PSRA (Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture), was therefore established. Its objective is to develop a cheaper, lighter, and more efficient retrieval system capable of recovering the containers already deployed on the planetary surface.


Participants must turn this concept into a successful sample-return mission.


Player Objectives
Cost-Effective Spacecraft Design: Build a lightweight spacecraft capable of landing, retrieving samples, and returning them to Earth. Minimize additional components to remain within the mission budget.
Precision Landing: Land near the ancient lake shorelines where sample containers are located, accounting for uneven terrain and tholin dust accumulation.
Sample Retrieval: Deploy a robotic collection system or small rover to retrieve the sealed containers and transport them to the landing platform.
Equipment Protection: Prevent dust accumulation on mechanical joints, moving components, and power systems, as it can reduce equipment efficiency and solar panel performance.
Surface Ascent: Transfer the samples into the ascent vehicle, complete system checks, and launch before approaching dust storms threaten the operation.
Orbital Rendezvous and Docking: Establish the required orbit and successfully dock with the waiting orbital spacecraft to transfer the samples.
Earth Return: Secure the samples inside a protected return capsule and complete atmospheric re-entry and landing while preventing contamination.


Main Gameplay Challenge
Complete a complex, multistage sample-return operation within a strictly limited budget.
Participants must coordinate five interconnected mission stages:
1. Planetary landing
2. Sample retrieval
3. Surface ascent and launch
4. Orbital rendezvous and docking
5. Earth return


The main challenges involve limited resources, dust storms, operational coordination, and maintaining scientific sample integrity.
The priority is to preserve the scientific achievements of the expedition, even if the exploration robot itself cannot survive.





Mission 4 – Hermeos-Mora
Story and Scientific Background


Hermeos-Mora is an original, scientifically modelled planetary environment representing one of the most extreme exploration scenarios in the project's planetary system.
It is characterized by exceptionally high atmospheric pressure, extreme temperatures, and intense tectonic and volcanic activity. Its modelled atmosphere consists predominantly of carbon dioxide (CO₂), alongside chemically active substances and upper atmospheric clouds containing

liquid sulfur dioxide droplets.
These conditions make conventional exploration spacecraft unsuitable for prolonged surface operations. Even specialized landers can function only briefly before their electronic systems and external components begin to deteriorate. 
    Nevertheless, Hermeos-Mora provides an opportunity to investigate volcanic processes, planetary chemical evolution, and extreme atmospheric conditions.


To study these phenomena, the MORA-13 Research Programme was established. Instead of conventional landers, the programme employs specialized robotic units equipped with reinforced thermal protection and active cooling systems.


According to the engineering calculations established for this planetary scenario, these protective systems can maintain operational functionality for a maximum of 30 minutes after landing.


Participants must conduct the scientific investigation within this limited timeframe and transmit essential data to an orbital relay before environmental conditions cause equipment failure.


Player Objectives
Research Robot Design: Construct a specialized exploration robot equipped with heat-resistant protection, active cooling, cameras, a drilling mechanism, a spectrometer, and microphones. Consider its mass and energy consumption in relation to its limited operational lifetime.
Atmospheric Descent: Perform a controlled descent through the dense atmosphere, deploying and releasing the parachute at the appropriate stages before activating the final braking system.
Precision Landing: Identify a relatively stable landing area, avoiding geological fractures, unstable tectonic regions, and hazardous volcanic formations.
Panoramic Imaging: Capture the first detailed color photographs of the surface, focusing on volcanic formations, thermally altered terrain, and atmospheric lighting before excessive heat damages the cameras.
Geological Sampling: Obtain a volcanic rock sample using the onboard drilling mechanism and analyze its chemical and mineral composition with an X-ray spectrometer.
Acoustic Data Collection: Record atmospheric sounds, volcanic activity, and seismic vibrations using protected microphones to investigate the planet's physical processes.
Scientific Data Transmission: Establish communication with the orbital relay and transmit photographs, chemical analysis, acoustic recordings, and operational telemetry.
Expedition Management: Complete priority scientific operations and transmit essential data before the robot exceeds its critical operating temperature and becomes permanently disabled.
Main Gameplay Challenge
Collect and transmit the maximum amount of scientific data within a 30-minute operational window.
Participants must continuously monitor the robot's temperature, energy consumption, and equipment status while prioritizing scientific activities.
They must decide how to allocate the available time between imaging, sample collection, chemical analysis, acoustic observations, and data transmission.
Complete a complex, multistage sample-return operation within a strictly limited budget.


Unlike conventional exploration missions, the primary objective is not necessarily to preserve the robotic platform, but to ensure the successful collection and transmission of scientific results before equipment failure.
